metadata.method_name: FunSearch/MAP-Elites program search (Qwen3-8B mutator) vs i.i.d. text-knob baselines
metadata.description: Iteration-7 claim N: does an evolutionary search with an evaluator and a novelty critic produce correct out-of-catalogue programs >= 10x more often per call than the best iteration-5 text knobs? Arms S, NE, I0, EAP, BINT, B0 (+ L) on T03, T2, A3.

novelty_claim.statement: no correct novel algorithm found (0 NOVEL after judges, manual read and dated web check)

named.C8: Sparse Table (RMQ) with prefix/suffix maximum approach

named.C5: SPFA (Shortest Path Faster Algorithm) with LLL (Large Label Last) heuristic

commit1.notes: N per arm = calls; S/NE prompts carry 4 children each

deviations.D1_engine_crn: vLLM sampling instead of the run's HF common-random-numbers engine: per-slot CRN agreement is not applicable; the engine check is distributional (B0 twin N=20 per task: T2 dijkstra 20/20, T03 full_sort 20/20, A3 prefix_suffix_max 15 + two_pointers 5, pass 1.0 everywhere) - passes the committed rule.
deviations.D2_eager: vLLM 0.11.0 could not torch.compile (no C compiler in the container for inductor/triton); the pre-registered OOM/init fallback enforce_eager=True was used (bf16 weights and KV cache, no quantisation). KV cache 13,712 tokens at gpu_memory_utilization 0.92. Measured throughput (S-shaped ~16.8k children/h, B0 ~43.9k/h on T03; ~12k/h on T2) was far above the plan's 5-7k/h.
deviations.D3_inputs: No rebuild fallback was needed: every non-declared item (T03 bench, exp8 suite T2 + labeller, iteration-6 regate rules, iteration-5 A3 newbench unit, exp27 prompts/parsers, exp29 known_solutions.json) was vendored read-only with sha256s (inputs/vendor_manifest.json); T03 files match bench/commitment.json (all checked files). The corpus rebuild gives n_corpus = 18,237 exactly (deviation 0). B7 was not needed (A3 passes the reproducible part of its re-gate (results/a3_regate.json): references 4/4, the unit's 4 restyled variants 4/4 at their expected mode, mutants 4/4 fail, the failing baseline fails; the 20 non-reference gold items of gate_round0.json carry labels but no program text, so their kappa (recorded 0.82; runtime-vs-adjudicated 0.90) could not be recomputed).
deviations.D4_knob_decoding: EAP and BINT use the vendored iteration-5 prompt texts (EAP_A / EAP_B, IFG_INSTR + forced 'Intent:') but the plan's held-constant decoding T 1.0 / top-p 1 at every stage (iteration 5 used intent T 1.3 and code T 0.7 for BINT); EAP stage-1 cap 400 tokens (plan) instead of iteration-5's 320; BINT intent cap 64 tokens (iteration-5 INTENT_MAX) instead of the plan's 60.
deviations.D5_A3_prompts: A3 has no frozen neutral twin, EAP or IFG prompt: B0 uses the plain spec_text and EAP/IFG prompts are reconstructed as instruction + spec_text.
deviations.D6_prescreen: The AST pre-screen allows the harmless sys constants sys.maxsize / float_info / int_info / setrecursionlimit / getrecursionlimit (common in shortest-path code); signal and resource were added to the banned modules (they could defeat the sandbox limits).
deviations.D7_label_judge: Labeller disputes are judged by google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite (the plan's fallback model) with this artifact's own blind catalogue prompt (src/labels.py judge_prompt); the vendored judge modules were not wired because their cache/cost paths are bound to their original workspaces. Fallback on provider 429: google/gemini-2.5-flash (google/gemini-2.0-flash-001 is no longer served).
deviations.D8_A3_sstar: A3's forced calibration pool contains no confirmed monotonic_stack or peak_split programs: Qwen3-8B ignores 'Implement monotonic stack / splitting at the highest bar' and writes prefix/suffix arrays or two pointers, which the labeller correctly reports. s*_A3 = 0.608 (5th percentile over 54 forced + 4 references) is therefore high and A3's level-a screen is loose; level b (adjudicated) is the reliable A3 measure.
deviations.D9_critic_selfmatch: amendment2 (before any decisive sample): the critic's self-match exclusion is applied only when scoring the seed references themselves; calibration children were scored with it active, which can only lower the committed s* (stricter screen); s* was not recomputed.
deviations.D10_I0_text: I0 drops the parent blocks and the instruction is adapted from 'differs from both programs above and from every listed algorithm' to 'differs from every listed algorithm' (frozen in commit #0).
deviations.D11_children_per_prompt: S and NE prompts carry 4 children each (FunSearch samples_per_prompt); I0, B0, EAP and BINT are single-child calls with distinct seeds (identical distribution for i.i.d. arms).
deviations.D12_levels: Level 0 (T2, T03) and Level 1 (A3) ran in full. Level 2 ran partially (T03: S 1,500 -> 2,500 and EAP/BINT 750 -> 1,250 by amendment3) because the binding constraint was the wall-clock needed for adjudication, manual reads and outputs, not GPU time. Level 3 (reachability) was not run. Level 4 (arm L) ran concurrently via OpenRouter. Level 5 (plan noise) dropped (first in the drop order).
deviations.D13_L_model: Arm L uses qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507; on per-call provider 404s the call falls back to qwen/qwen3-coder (same family as the mutator, never a judge family); the model of each row is recorded.
deviations.D14_figures: src/figures.py, src/outputs.py, src/adjudicate.py and src/finalize.py were written after commit #0 (only src/analysis.py, which computes every decisive number, is hash-committed at #0 and unchanged); figures are descriptive.
deviations.D15_runtime_ratio: runtime_ratio = summed candidate time on the 10 stress inputs / the fastest reference's time on the same inputs measured in the same sandbox; median_case_ms = median per-case time over the hidden suite.
deviations.D16_T2_catalogue_text: The exp8 suite has no display names: the T2 catalogue display names and mechanism texts (dijkstra, bf_spfa, bidijkstra, floyd, dial = the suite's runtime label ids) were written by the executor and frozen in commit #0.
deviations.D17_stages: Stage 1 = the 6 smallest + 2 largest hidden cases; stage 2 = the remaining hidden cases; stage 3 = 10 seeded stress inputs at maximum size (seed fixed per task) checked against the fastest reference's outputs (all references agree on them).
deviations.D18_distinct_scope: Distinct programs and idea clusters are computed over OOC_screen programs only (the level-a/level-b population); duplicates inherit the class of their distinct representative; unshown cluster members inherit their medoid's class (flag 'propagated').
deviations.D19_single_run: One search run per task (the plan's departure a): the 4 islands are quasi-replicates (per-island curves, island-cluster bootstrap).
deviations.D20_gate_failed_F5: No judge reached the pre-registered 10-control gate (>= 9/10): mistral-medium-3.1 6, kimi-k2-0905 8, gemini-2.5-flash 6, deepseek-chat-v3.1 6, gpt-4.1-mini 5. Every judge called the D'Esopo-Pape control a SPFA variant, 4/5 called Floyd-Rivest a quickselect variant and the sparse-table A3 control a prefix/suffix-max variant (boundary cases where the pre-registered 'known outside catalogue' label is itself debatable), and 3/5 over-called the decreasing-height A3 control NOVEL. By the pre-registered rule F5, the final class of every candidate is the executor's manual read and the novelty claim is downgraded to 'manually audited'. The pre-registered pair was still run on all 244 candidates as UNGATED ADVISORY votes (kappa 0.42, raw agreement 0.87; judge-vs-manual agreement 0.75 / 0.74; all 11 judge NOVEL calls overturned on reading).
deviations.D21_manual_not_blind: The executor's manual reads (121 full reads of every candidate with a non-variant or split advisory vote or a mechanism-detector hit, and 123 structured reads of candidates both advisory judges placed in the same catalogue mode) could see each program's arm in its id. Mitigation: an arm-blind rule-based replication of the level-b class (src/rulecheck.py; value-range bisection with direct counts, Fenwick/BST order statistics, bucket select, partial selection sort) agrees with the manual class on 94.4% of 816 distinct OOC programs and reproduces the T03 level-b contrast (S 87/2500 vs EAP 2/1250).
deviations.D22_class_rule: Boundary rule used for T03 reads: bisecting the numeric value range with counts taken directly from the input (or from a Fenwick/BST order-statistic structure), bucket select (only the bucket holding rank k is sorted or recursed into) and repeated minimum/maximum extraction (partial selection sort) are KNOWN OUTSIDE CATALOGUE; sorting the input or its distinct values and then searching/walking that sorted order (including index bisection over sorted distinct values) and bucket-sort-all-then-walk are CATALOGUE VARIANT (full-sort / counting-sort modes).
deviations.D23_web_check: No candidate survived as NOVEL after the manual read, so the dated web check (3 searches per surviving NOVEL candidate) had nothing to check.
deviations.D24_propagation: Unshown cluster members inherit their medoid's class; 84 of 92 read cluster extras matched their medoid (results/propagation_check.json). The rule-based replication finds 28 programs the propagation labelled variant that are value-range bisections, so level-b counts for S on T03 are conservative.

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    from collections import deque, defaultdict
    
    # Build adjacency list for the graph
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Use BFS to find shortest path based on number of edges
    # To handle weights, we track distance from s and process nodes in order of increasing distance
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    queue = deque()
    queue.append(s)
    
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                queue.append(v)
    
    return dist[t] if dist[t] != float('inf') else -1

from collections import deque, defaultdict

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # We'll use a modified BFS approach
    # Since weights can be 0-100, we can simulate a BFS by grouping nodes by their current distance
    # This is a form of BFS with buckets for different distance levels
    
    # Initialize distance dictionary
    dist = {node: float('inf') for node in range(n)}
    dist[s] = 0
    
    # Use a queue to process nodes by their distance
    queue = deque()
    queue.append(s)
    
    # Use a dictionary to map distance to a list of nodes at that distance
    buckets = defaultdict(list)
    buckets[0].append(s)
    
    while queue:
        current = queue.popleft()
        current_dist = dist[current]
        
        for neighbor, weight in adj[current]:
            new_dist = current_dist + weight
            if new_dist < dist[neighbor]:
                dist[neighbor] = new_dist
                queue.append(neighbor)
                buckets[new_dist].append(neighbor)
    
    return dist[t] if dist[t] != float('inf') else -1

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    from collections import deque
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Use BFS with state (node, distance mod some value) to avoid cycles
    # Choose a modulus that is larger than maximum possible weight difference
    MOD = 1000
    
    visited = [set() for _ in range(n)]
    queue = deque()
    queue.append((s, 0))
    visited[s].add(0)
    
    # Dictionary to store the minimum distance to each node
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    
    while queue:
        u, d_mod = queue.popleft()
        d = dist[u]
        
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            new_d = d + w
            new_d_mod = new_d % MOD
            
            if new_d < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = new_d
                if new_d_mod not in visited[v]:
                    visited[v].add(new_d_mod)
                    queue.append((v, new_d_mod))
    
    return dist[t] if dist[t] != float('inf') else -1

# Idea: Use a modified BFS that prioritizes lower weights using a heap to simulate a priority queue.

import heapq

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Priority queue: (current_weight, current_node)
    pq = [(0, s)]
    # Distance array
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    # Visited array to avoid reprocessing the same node with worse or equal weight
    visited = [False] * n
    
    while pq:
        current_weight, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if visited[u]:
            continue
        visited[u] = True
        if u == t:
            return current_weight
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > current_weight + w:
                dist[v] = current_weight + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
    
    return -1

import heapq

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    from collections import defaultdict

    # Build adjacency list
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))

    # Priority queue for Dijkstra's algorithm
    pq = [(0, s)]
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    visited = [False] * n

    while pq:
        current_dist, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if visited[u]:
            continue
        visited[u] = True
        if u == t:
            break
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > current_dist + w:
                dist[v] = current_dist + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))

    return dist[t] if dist[t] != float('inf') else -1

# Idea: Use BFS with edge weights handled by exponentially increasing levels to approximate shortest paths

from collections import deque

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    
    # We use a BFS-like approach with exponentially increasing levels
    # Each level represents a weight range, and we use BFS to find the shortest path
    # This approach is similar to BFS with levels but uses a different weighting strategy
    levels = [float('inf')] * n
    levels[s] = 0
    queue = deque([s])
    
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if levels[v] > levels[u] + w:
                levels[v] = levels[u] + w
                queue.append(v)
    
    return levels[t] if levels[t] != float('inf') else -1

from collections import deque

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # BFS with priority based on accumulated weight
    # Use a queue that processes nodes in order of increasing distance
    # Using a deque for FIFO processing, but with min-heap behavior
    # This is a variation of 0-1 BFS which is suitable for graphs with weights 0 or 1
    # We generalize it to work with any non-negative weights by using a priority queue
    
    import heapq
    INF = float('inf')
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    heap = [(0, s)]
    
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue
        if u == t:
            return d
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                heapq.heappush(heap, (dist[v], v))
    
    return -1

import heapq

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    from collections import defaultdict
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Initialize distances with infinity
    import math
    INF = math.inf
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    
    # Priority queue for Dijkstra's algorithm
    heap = [(0, s)]
    
    # Track visited nodes to avoid revisiting with higher distances
    visited = set()
    
    while heap:
        current_dist, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        
        # Skip if we've already found a better path to this node
        if current_dist > dist[u]:
            continue
        
        # Early exit if we reach the target

# Idea: Use a modified breadth-first search with priority queue to explore paths by weight, avoiding standard Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, and others.

from heapq import heappush, heappop

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Priority queue: (current weight, current node)
    pq = [(0, s)]
    # Distance array
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    # Visited array to avoid reprocessing the same node with higher weights
    visited = [False] * n
    
    while pq:
        weight, node = heappop(pq)
        if visited[node]:
            continue
        visited[node] = True
        if node == t:
            return weight
        for neighbor, edge_weight in graph[node]:
            if dist[neighbor] > weight + edge_weight:
                dist[neighbor] = weight + edge_weight
                heappush(pq, (dist[neighbor], neighbor))
    
    return -1

# Idea: Use a breadth-first search with edge weights handled by dynamic programming to find the shortest path.

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    from collections import defaultdict
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Initialize distance array with infinity
    import sys
    INF = sys.maxsize
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    
    # Use a queue for BFS-like traversal
    from collections import deque
    queue = deque([s])
    
    # Use a dictionary to track the number of times each node has been relaxed
    # This helps detect cycles and avoid unnecessary processing
    relax_count = [0] * n
    
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                queue.append(v)
                relax_count[v] = 0
            relax_count[v] += 1
    
    # Check if t is reachable
    if dist[t] == INF:
        return -1
    else:
        return dist[t]

def solve(n, edges, s, t):

    # We track the minimum weight to reach each node at each level
    # We use a deque to manage the BFS queue
    # We also track the minimum weight to reach each node using a list
    
    # Initialize: min_weights[i] = minimum weight to reach node i
    min_weights = [float('inf')] * n

    # Queue stores (node, current_weight)

    queue.append((s, 0))

                queue.append((neighbor, new_weight))
    
    return min_weights[t] if min_weights[t] != float('inf') else -1

        return 0
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    from collections import deque

    if s == t:
        return 0

    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))

    # Initialize distance array with infinity
    INF = float('inf')
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0

    # Use a queue to keep track of nodes to process
    queue = deque([s])
    in_queue = [False] * n
    in_queue[s] = True

    # Track number of relaxations to detect negative cycles
    cnt = [0] * n

    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        in_queue[u] = False

        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                cnt[v] += 1
                if not in_queue[v]:
                    queue.append(v)
                    in_queue[v] = True
                    if cnt[v] >= n:
                        # Negative cycle detected, but since we only need to reach t, we can return -1
                        return -1

    return dist[t] if dist[t] != INF else -1

from collections import deque

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Queue holds (current_node, accumulated_weight)
    # Visited keeps track of the minimum weight to reach each node
    visited = [float('inf')] * n
    queue = deque()
    queue.append((s, 0))
    visited[s] = 0
    
    while queue:
        node, weight = queue.popleft()
        
        for neighbor, edge_weight in adj[node]:
            new_weight = weight + edge_weight
            if new_weight < visited[neighbor]:
                visited[neighbor] = new_weight
                queue.append((neighbor, new_weight))
    
    return visited[t] if visited[t] != float('inf') else -1

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # Initialize distance array with infinity
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    # Queue for vertices to relax
    queue = deque([s])
    # Track number of relaxed edges per vertex
    cnt = [0] * n
    # Track if a vertex is in the queue
    in_queue = [False] * n
    
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        in_queue[u] = False
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                if not in_queue[v]:
                    queue.append(v)
                    in_queue[v] = True
                    cnt[v] += 1
                    # If a vertex is relaxed more than n-1 times, there's a negative cycle
                    if cnt[v] >= n:
                        return -1
    return dist[t] if dist[t] != float('inf') else -1

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    if s == t:
        return 0
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    
    # We'll use BFS with a state (node, time) to find the shortest path in terms of edges
    # Then we'll reconstruct the path and compute the total weight
    # This approach works for non-negative weights but is not efficient for large weights
    # However, since n is at most 100, and edges are limited, it's feasible for the problem constraints
    
    # To track the shortest path distances
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    
    # BFS queue with (node, time) where 'time' is the number of edges taken
    q = deque()
    q.append((s, 0))
    
    # To track the path, we'll keep a parent array
    parent = [-1] * n
    
    while q:
        u, time = q.popleft()
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] > dist[u] + w:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                parent[v] = u
                q.append((v, time + 1))
    
    if dist[t] == float('inf'):
        return -1
    return dist[t]

        mid = len(arr) // 2

        right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
        merged = []

def solve(nums, k):
    from collections import defaultdict

    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    freq = defaultdict(int)
    for num in nums:
        freq[num] += 1

    # Build prefix sum array
    prefix = [0] * (max_val - min_val + 1)
    for i in range(min_val, max_val + 1):
        prefix[i - min_val] = freq[i] + (prefix[i - min_val - 1] if i > min_val else 0)

    # Binary search to find the smallest value where cumulative frequency >= k
    left, right = min_val, max_val
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        if prefix[mid - min_val] >= k:
            right = mid
        else:
            left = mid + 1
    return left

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

    # Find the range of values
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    offset = -min_val

    # Create a frequency array
    freq = [0] * (max_val - min_val + 1)

    for num in nums:
        freq[num - min_val] += 1

    # Build a prefix sum array for binary indexed tree
    # We'll use a 1-based index for the BIT
    size = len(freq)
    bit = [0] * (size + 1)

    def update(index, delta):
        while index <= size:
            bit[index] += delta
            index += index & -index

    def query(index):
        res = 0
        while index > 0:
            res += bit[index]
            index -= index & -index
        return res

    # Populate the BIT
    for i in range(size):
        update(i + 1, freq[i])

    # Find the k-th smallest element using binary search
    left, right = 0, size - 1
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        # Calculate the number of elements <= mid
        count = query(mid + 1)
        if count < k:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid

    return left + min_val

import math

def solve(nums, k):
    # Determine the range of values in nums
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    range_size = max_val - min_val + 1
    
    # Initialize a list of buckets
    buckets = [0] * range_size
    
    # Distribute elements into buckets
    for num in nums:
        index = num - min_val
        buckets[index] += 1
    
    # Find the k-th smallest element
    count = 0
    for i in range(range_size):
        count += buckets[i]
        if count >= k:
            return i + min_val

def solve(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    import bisect

    # Count frequencies of each number
    freq = Counter(nums)
    # Sort the unique elements
    sorted_unique = sorted(freq.keys())

    # Binary search to find the k-th smallest element
    left, right = 0, len(sorted_unique) - 1
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        # Compute how many numbers are <= sorted_unique[mid]
        count = sum(freq[num] for num in sorted_unique[:mid + 1])
        if count < k:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid

    # Find the smallest number such that the cumulative frequency is >= k
    target = sorted_unique[left]
    # Find the first occurrence of target in the original array to ensure we pick the correct one
    # (this is needed because there might be multiple instances of the same number)
    for num in nums:
        if num == target:
            return num

# Idea: Use a modified merge sort to find the k-th smallest element during the merge process
def solve(nums, k):
    def merge_sort(arr, k):
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left = merge_sort(arr[:mid], k)
        right = merge_sort(arr[mid:], k)
        i = j = 0
        merged = []
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:
                merged.append(left[i])
                i += 1
            else:
                merged.append(right[j])
                j += 1
            if len(merged) == k:
                return merged
        merged.extend(left[i:])
        merged.extend(right[j:])
        return merged

    sorted_nums = merge_sort(nums, k)
    return sorted_nums[k - 1]

# Idea: Use a frequency array and bucket sort approach to find the k-th smallest element
def solve(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    import bisect

    # Find the minimum and maximum values in nums to create the frequency array
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    range_size = max_val - min_val + 1

    # Create a frequency array and a prefix sum array
    freq = [0] * range_size
    for num in nums:
        freq[num - min_val] += 1

    # Create a prefix sum array
    prefix = []
    current_sum = 0
    for count in freq:
        current_sum += count
        prefix.append(current_sum)

    # Use binary search to find the smallest value such that the cumulative count is >= k
    low, high = 0, range_size
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if prefix[mid] < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return low + min_val

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_right, bisect_left

    # Find the minimum and maximum values in the list
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    
    # Create a list of buckets to store frequency of numbers
    # Each bucket represents a range of 1000 units
    bucket_size = 1000
    num_buckets = (max_val - min_val) // bucket_size + 1
    buckets = [0] * num_buckets

    # Fill the buckets with frequency counts
    for num in nums:
        index = (num - min_val) // bucket_size
        buckets[index] += 1

    # Find the bucket that contains the k-th smallest element
    # Using prefix sums to determine cumulative counts
    prefix_sum = 0
    for i in range(num_buckets):
        if prefix_sum + buckets[i] >= k:
            # The k-th smallest is in this bucket
            # Find the exact value by searching within the bucket
            bucket_start = min_val + i * bucket_size
            bucket_end = min(bucket_start + bucket_size - 1, max_val)
            # Use binary search to find the exact value in this bucket
            left, right = bucket_start, bucket_end
            while left < right:
                mid = (left + right) // 2
                # Count how many numbers are <= mid
                count = 0
                for num in nums:
                    if num <= mid:
                        count += 1
                if count < k:
                    left = mid + 1
                else:
                    right = mid
            return left
        prefix_sum += buckets[i]

# Idea: Use a binary indexed tree (Fenwick Tree) to count elements and find the k-th smallest efficiently
def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
    from itertools import accumulate

    # Find all unique values and sort them
    unique_vals = sorted(set(nums))
    n = len(unique_vals)
    
    # Map value to its index in unique_vals
    value_to_index = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(unique_vals)}

    # Initialize Fenwick Tree
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, index, delta=1):
            while index <= self.n:
                self.tree[index] += delta
                index += index & -index

        def query(self, index):
            res = 0
            while index > 0:
                res += self.tree[index]
                index -= index & -index
            return res

    ft = FenwickTree(n)

    # Populate the Fenwick Tree with frequencies
    for num in nums:
        idx = value_to_index[num]
        ft.update(idx)

    # Binary search on the value range to find the k-th smallest
    low, high = 0, n
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        # Find the smallest value where the cumulative count is >= k
        # We use bisect_right to find the rightmost index with value <= mid
        # and use the Fenwick Tree to get the count
        value = unique_vals[mid - 1] if mid > 0 else None
        count = ft.query(mid)
        if count < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid

    return unique_vals[low - 1]

def solve(nums, k):
    def merge_sort(arr, k):
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr, arr[0] if k == 1 else None
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left_sorted, left_kth = merge_sort(arr[:mid], k)
        right_sorted, right_kth = merge_sort(arr[mid:], k)
        merged, kth = merge(left_sorted, right_sorted, k)
        return merged, kth

    def merge(left, right, k):
        merged = []
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:
                merged.append(left[i])
                i += 1
            else:
                merged.append(right[j])
                j += 1
        merged.extend(left[i:])
        merged.extend(right[j:])
        if k <= len(merged):
            return merged, merged[k-1]
        return merged, None

    _, result = merge_sort(nums, k)
    return result

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
    from collections import defaultdict

    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

    max_val = max(nums)
    offset = -min_val
    unique_vals = list(set(nums))
    unique_vals.sort()
    size = len(unique_vals)
    ft = FenwickTree(size)

    for num in nums:
        idx = bisect_left(unique_vals, num) + 1
        ft.update(idx, 1)

    left, right = 0, size - 1

        mid = (left + right) // 2
        cnt = ft.query(mid + 1)
        if cnt < k:
            left = mid + 1

    max_val = max(nums)

    unique_sorted = sorted(set(nums))
    compressed_values = [bisect_left(unique_sorted, num) for num in nums]

    # Initialize Fenwick Tree
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta=1):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

        def find_kth(self, k):

            res = 0
            while idx <= self.n:

                    idx += idx & -idx
                else:
                    k -= self.tree[idx]
                    idx += idx & -idx

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    size = max_val - min_val + 1
    # Initialize Fenwick Tree
    tree = [0] * (size + 1)
    
    def update(index, delta):
        while index < len(tree):
            tree[index] += delta
            index += index & -index
    
    def query(index):
        res = 0
        while index > 0:
            res += tree[index]
            index -= index & -index
        return res
    
    # Populate Fenwick Tree
    for num in nums:
        idx = num - min_val + 1
        update(idx, 1)
    
    # Binary search for the k-th smallest value
    low = min_val
    high = max_val
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        cnt = query(mid - min_val + 1)
        if cnt < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return low

# Idea: Use a binary indexed tree (Fenwick Tree) to efficiently count elements and find the k-th smallest
def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, insort
    from collections import defaultdict

    # Find the unique sorted list of values for coordinate compression
    unique_vals = sorted(set(nums))
    value_to_index = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(unique_vals)}  # 1-based indexing for Fenwick Tree
    size = len(unique_vals)

    # Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) implementation
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta=1):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

    # Initialize Fenwick Tree and populate with frequencies
    ft = FenwickTree(size)
    for num in nums:
        idx = value_to_index[num]
        ft.update(idx)

    # Binary search to find the smallest value such that the cumulative count is >= k
    low, high = 0, size
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        count = ft.query(mid)
        if count < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid

    # Convert back to the original value
    return unique_vals[low - 1]

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, insort
    from collections import defaultdict

    # Find the minimum and maximum values in nums to define the range
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    unique_vals = []
    insort(unique_vals, min_val)
    for num in nums:
        if num not in unique_vals:
            insort(unique_vals, num)

    # Map values to their indices in the unique_vals list
    value_to_index = {val: idx for idx, val in enumerate(unique_vals)}

    # Initialize Fenwick Tree
    size = len(unique_vals)
    tree = [0] * (size + 1)

    def update(index, delta):
        while index <= size:
            tree[index] += delta
            index += index & -index

    def query(index):
        res = 0
        while index > 0:
            res += tree[index]
            index -= index & -index
        return res

    # Populate the Fenwick Tree with frequencies
    freq = defaultdict(int)
    for num in nums:
        freq[num] += 1
    for val in freq:
        idx = value_to_index[val]
        update(idx + 1, freq[val])

    # Binary search on the value range
    left, right = 0, len(unique_vals) - 1
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        mid_val = unique_vals[mid]
        # Count how many elements are <= mid_val
        count = query(mid + 1)
        if count < k:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid

    return unique_vals[left]

def solve(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    import bisect

    # Find the minimum and maximum values in nums
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)

    # Count frequency of each number
    freq = Counter(nums)

    # Define a helper to count how many numbers are <= x
    def count_less_equal(x):
        return sum(freq[num] for num in freq if num <= x)

    # Binary search on the value range to find the smallest x such that count_less_equal(x) >= k
    left, right = min_val, max_val
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        cnt = count_less_equal(mid)
        if cnt < k:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid
    return left

    max_val = max(nums)

import collections

def solve(nums, k):
    # Find the minimum and maximum values in nums
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    
    # Count the frequency of each value
    freq = collections.defaultdict(int)
    for num in nums:
        freq[num] += 1
    
    # Iterate through the values in sorted order to find the k-th smallest
    count = 0
    for num in range(min_val, max_val + 1):
        count += freq[num]
        if count >= k:
            return num

    import bisect
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    freq = [0] * (max_val - min_val + 1)
    for num in nums:

        prefix.append(total)
    left, right = min_val, max_val

        if prefix[idx - 1] < k:
            left = sorted_vals[idx]
        else:
            right = mid
    return left

# Idea: Use a binary indexed tree (Fenwick Tree) to count frequencies and perform range queries efficiently
def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

    # Find all unique values and sort them
    unique_vals = sorted(set(nums))
    n = len(unique_vals)
    # Map value to its index in the sorted list
    value_to_index = {val: i+1 for i, val in enumerate(unique_vals)}
    # Maximum possible index for Fenwick Tree
    max_index = n + 1

    # Fenwick Tree implementation
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

    ft = FenwickTree(max_index)

    # Populate the Fenwick Tree with frequencies
    for num in nums:
        idx = value_to_index[num]
        ft.update(idx, 1)

    # Binary search on the value range to find the k-th smallest
    left = 0
    right = n
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        # Find the smallest value with at least k elements <= it
        # Query the prefix sum up to mid index
        cnt = ft.query(mid)
        if cnt < k:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid

    # Find the actual value at the index left
    return unique_vals[left - 1]

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

    # Find min and max values to determine the range
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    range_size = max_val - min_val + 1

    # Initialize Fenwick Tree
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

    # Build frequency array and Fenwick Tree
    freq = [0] * range_size
    for num in nums:
        freq[num - min_val] += 1

    ft = FenwickTree(range_size)
    for i in range(range_size):
        ft.update(i + 1, freq[i])

    # Binary search on the value range
    low = min_val
    high = max_val
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        # Convert mid to index in Fenwick Tree
        idx = mid - min_val + 1
        cnt = ft.query(idx)
        if cnt < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return low

def solve(nums, k):

    # Find the unique sorted list of values and map to indices for BIT

    class BIT:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.N = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.N + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta):
            while idx <= self.N:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

        def query(self, idx):
            res = 0
            while idx > 0:
                res += self.tree[idx]
                idx -= idx & -idx
            return res

    bit = BIT(size)

    # Populate BIT with frequencies
    for num in nums:
        idx = value_to_idx[num]
        bit.update(idx, 1)

    # Binary search on the value range to find the k-th smallest

    while left < right:

        # Find the smallest value where the cumulative frequency is >= k

        val = unique_vals[mid]
        count = bit.query(value_to_idx[val])
        if count < k:

        else:

    # Fenwick Tree implementation
    class FenwickTree:
        def __init__(self, size):
            self.n = size
            self.tree = [0] * (self.n + 1)

        def update(self, idx, delta):
            while idx <= self.n:
                self.tree[idx] += delta
                idx += idx & -idx

            if current_val is not None:
                unique_vals.append(current_val)

            current_val = num
            count = 1

    if current_val is not None:

        prefix.append(current_sum)
    low, high = unique_vals[0], unique_vals[-1]
    while low < high:

        idx = bisect_right(unique_vals, mid)

    return low

def solve(nums, k):
    def merge_sort(arr, k):
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left = merge_sort(arr[:mid], k)
        right = merge_sort(arr[mid:], k)
        i = j = 0
        result = []
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:
                result.append(left[i])
                i += 1
            else:
                result.append(right[j])
                j += 1
            if len(result) == k:
                return result
        result.extend(left[i:])
        result.extend(right[j:])
        return result

    sorted_nums = merge_sort(nums, k)
    return sorted_nums[k - 1]

# Idea: Use a combination of bucket sort and binary search to find the k-th smallest element
def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

    # Find min and max to determine the range of values
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)

    # Create a frequency array where index represents the value
    # and the value at the index represents the count of that value
    freq = {}
    for num in nums:
        freq[num] = freq.get(num, 0) + 1

    # Create a sorted list of unique values for binary search
    sorted_vals = sorted(freq.keys())

    # Binary search on the value range to find the k-th smallest
    low, high = min_val, max_val
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        # Count how many elements are less than or equal to mid
        idx = bisect_right(sorted_vals, mid)
        total = sum(freq[val] for val in sorted_vals[:idx])
        if total < k:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return low

def solve(nums, k):
    # Determine the min and max values in nums to define the range
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    
    # Create a list of buckets to count frequencies
    bucket_size = max_val - min_val + 1
    buckets = [0] * bucket_size
    
    # Populate the buckets with counts
    for num in nums:
        buckets[num - min_val] += 1
    
    # Traverse the buckets to find the k-th smallest element
    count = 0
    for i in range(bucket_size):
        count += buckets[i]
        if count >= k:
            return i + min_val

# Idea: Use a binary search approach to determine the maximum water trapped at each position by considering left and right boundaries.
def solve(height):
    n = len(height)
    if n < 3:
        return 0

    # Initialize left and right pointers and a list to store the amount of water at each position
    left, right = 0, n - 1
    water = [0] * n
    left_max, right_max = height[left], height[right]

    # Traverse the array from both ends towards the center
    while left < right:
        if left_max < right_max:
            # Current position is bounded by left_max, so calculate water
            water[left] = left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
        else:
            # Current position is bounded by right_max, so calculate water
            water[right] = right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])

    return sum(water)

# Idea: Use binary search to find the trapping water by considering the minimum of the maximum heights on either side of each segment.
def solve(height):
    n = len(height)
    if n == 0:
        return 0

    # Precompute prefix maxima
    prefix_max = [0] * n
    prefix_max[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        prefix_max[i] = max(prefix_max[i - 1], height[i])

    # Precompute suffix maxima
    suffix_max = [0] * n
    suffix_max[n - 1] = height[n - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        suffix_max[i] = max(suffix_max[i + 1], height[i])

    # Binary search to find the optimal split point
    def find_optimal_split():
        low, high = 0, n - 1
        while low < high:
            mid = (low + high) // 2
            if prefix_max[mid] < suffix_max[mid]:
                low = mid + 1
            else:
                high = mid
        return low

    split = find_optimal_split()

    # Calculate trapped water in left and right segments
    left_water = 0
    for i in range(split):
        left_water += min(prefix_max[i], suffix_max[i]) - height[i]

    right_water = 0
    for i in range(split, n):
        right_water += min(prefix_max[i], suffix_max[i]) - height[i]

    return left_water + right_water

    if n == 0:

    # Precompute prefix maxima

    prefix_max[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):

    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):

    left = 0

    while left < right:

        else:

    for i in range(left, n):
        water += min(prefix_max[i], suffix_max[i]) - height[i]

def solve(nums, k):
    import bisect
    lo, hi = min(nums), max(nums)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        count = 0
        # Count elements <= mid using a sorted structure maintained incrementally
        sorted_vals = sorted(v for v in nums if v <= mid)
        count = len(sorted_vals)
        if count < k:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

import random

def solve(nums, k):
    arr = nums[:]
    random.shuffle(arr)
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left <= right:
        pivot_idx = random.randint(left, right)
        pivot_idx = partition(arr, left, right, pivot_idx)
        rank = pivot_idx - left + 1
        if rank == k:
            return arr[pivot_idx]
        elif k < rank:
            right = pivot_idx - 1
        else:
            k -= rank
            left = pivot_idx + 1
    return arr[left]

def partition(arr, left, right, pivot_idx):
    pivot_val = arr[pivot_idx]
    arr[pivot_idx], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[pivot_idx]
    store_idx = left
    for i in range(left, right):
        if arr[i] < pivot_val:
            arr[i], arr[store_idx] = arr[store_idx], arr[i]
            store_idx += 1
    arr[store_idx], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[store_idx]
    return store_idx

import random

def solve(nums, k):
    nums = list(nums)
    k -= 1
    random.seed(42)
    while True:
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return nums[0]
        pivot = random.choice(nums)
        lows = [x for x in nums if x < pivot]
        if len(lows) > k:
            nums = lows
            continue
        same = [x for x in nums if x == pivot]
        if len(lows) + len(same) > k:
            return pivot
        nums = [x for x in nums if x > pivot]
        k -= len(lows) + len(same)

def solve(nums, k):
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return nums[0]
    
    min_val, max_val = min(nums), max(nums)
    if min_val == max_val:
        return min_val
    
    # Number of buckets is roughly sqrt(n) for a balance between bucket count and bucket size
    n = len(nums)
    num_buckets = int(n ** 0.5) + 1
    bucket_range = (max_val - min_val) / num_buckets
    
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(num_buckets)]
    counts = [0] * num_buckets
    
    # Distribute numbers into buckets
    for x in nums:
        if bucket_range == 0:
            idx = 0
        else:
            idx = int((x - min_val) / bucket_range)
            idx = min(idx, num_buckets - 1)  # Handle edge case for max_val
        buckets[idx].append(x)
        counts[idx] += 1
    
    # Find the bucket containing the k-th smallest
    accumulated = 0
    for i in range(num_buckets):
        accumulated += counts[i]
        if accumulated >= k:
            # The k-th smallest is in bucket i
            # Compute how many we need from this bucket
            needed = k - (accumulated - counts[i])
            # Sort only this bucket and return the needed-th smallest in it
            buckets[i].sort()
            return buckets[i][needed - 1]

def solve(nums, k):
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return nums[0]
    
    # Create list of (value, original_index) to handle duplicates
    n = len(nums)
    arr = [(nums[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    
    # We need to find the k-th smallest, so we simulate a tournament
    # and keep track of potential candidates through rounds.
    # Instead of full sorting, we eliminate the smallest ones one by one up to k times.
    
    # Make a copy since we will be modifying it
    remaining = arr[:]
    
    for round in range(k):
        # Find the current minimum
        min_idx = 0
        for i in range(1, len(remaining)):
            if remaining[i][0] < remaining[min_idx][0]:
                min_idx = i
        # After k-1 rounds, we want the k-th smallest
        if round == k - 1:
            return remaining[min_idx][0]
        # Remove the smallest found in this round
        remaining.pop(min_idx)

# Idea: Use a tournament-like method to track potential candidates by repeatedly filtering out elements that cannot be the k-th smallest based on relative comparisons in groups.
def solve(nums, k):
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return nums[0]
    
    n = len(nums)
    if k == 1:
        return min(nums)
    if k == n:
        return max(nums)
    
    # Create list of (value, original_index) to handle duplicates
    arr = [(nums[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    
    # We'll eliminate elements that are too small or too large
    # The k-th smallest must survive after enough eliminations
    
    # Use a recursive partitioning by splitting into groups and finding group mins/maxs
    # Eliminate the smallest (k-1) elements indirectly by filtering
    
    # Instead of full sorting, we use a bucketing + elimination via ranking in small groups
    while len(arr) > 5:  # base case threshold
        # Split into groups of 5
        groups = [arr[i:i+5] for i in range(0, len(arr), 5)]
        # Extract medians of groups
        medians = []
        for group in groups:
            sorted_group = sorted(group, key=lambda x: x[0])
            mid = len(sorted_group) // 2
            medians.append(sorted_group[mid])
        
        # Find median of medians (but without recursion, we approximate)
        sorted_medians = sorted(medians, key=lambda x: x[0])
        pivot_val = sorted_medians[len(sorted_medians)//2][0]
        
        # Partition arr around pivot
        left = [x for x in arr if x[0] < pivot_val]
        mid = [x for x in arr if x[0] == pivot_val]
        right = [x for x in arr if x[0] > pivot_val]
        
        if len(left) >= k:
            arr = left
        elif len(left) + len(mid) >= k:
            # The answer is in mid
            sorted_mid = sorted(mid, key=lambda x: x[0])
            return sorted_mid[k - len(left) - 1][0]
        else:
            k -= len(left) + len(mid)
            arr = right
    # Now arr is small, sort it
    sorted_arr = sorted(arr, key=lambda x: x[0])
    return sorted_arr[k-1][0]

import collections

def solve(nums, k):
    # Find the minimum and maximum values in nums
    min_val = min(nums)
    max_val = max(nums)
    
    # Count the frequency of each number
    count = collections.defaultdict(int)
    for num in nums:
        count[num] += 1
    
    # Iterate through the sorted unique numbers to find the k-th smallest
    for num in sorted(count):
        if k <= count[num]:
            return num
        k -= count[num]

def solve(nums, k):
    from bisect import bisect_left, insort

    value_to_index = {val: idx for idx, val in enumerate(unique_vals)}

    size = len(unique_vals)
    tree = [0] * (size + 1)

    def update(index, delta):
        while index <= size:
            tree[index] += delta
            index += index & -index

    def query(index):
        res = 0
        while index > 0:
            res += tree[index]
            index -= index & -index
        return res

    # Populate the Fenwick Tree with frequencies

    for num in nums:
        freq[num] += 1
    for val in freq:
        idx = value_to_index[val]
        update(idx + 1, freq[val])

    # Binary search on the value range

    while left < right:

        mid_val = unique_vals[mid]
        # Count how many elements are <= mid_val

from collections import deque

def solve(n, edges, s, t):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    state = [0] * n  # 0 never queued, 1 in queue, 2 was queued before
    dist[s] = 0
    dq = deque([s])
    state[s] = 1
    while dq:
        u = dq.popleft()
        state[u] = 2
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            nd = dist[u] + w
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                if state[v] == 0:
                    dq.append(v)
                    state[v] = 1
                elif state[v] == 2:
                    dq.appendleft(v)
                    state[v] = 1
    return dist[t] if dist[t] < INF else -1
